In these attacks, an adversary secretly injects a trap into an AI model's parameters, enabling manipulated outputs when inputs contain hidden triggers while leaving legitimate functionality largely intact for untriggered data. Yet, an input containing only the backdoor trigger without the main attack payload often inadvertently exposes the system to additional manipulation, potentially revealing the attack's existence. Although existing research hints that increasing a Convolutional Neural Network's depth and width mitigates the risk of such attacks, these broader architectures remain computationally and memory-intensive. This paper introduces a novel approach to detect backdoor injections by utilizing standard Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). By leveraging the extensive pre-trained weights of an RNN trained for natural language processing, the model can identify inputs with triggers that lack semantic content, thereby catching the attack without consuming excessive processing power. Numerical simulations confirm the effectiveness of this proposed detection strategy.

Hubble constant, $H_0$, varies across different cosmic distances due to differences in expansion rates across varying regions. We present novel observations regarding the differential age of star-forming regions within galaxies that support these variations in $H_0$. Under the assumption of a cosmological Hubble flow, we demonstrate that under specific dark energy and dark matter density conditions, the differential formation or current ages of star clusters within galaxies can serve as a reliable indicator for estimating the inverse of the product of the Hubble parameter and square of the scale factor ($1/H(z)$). By applying our model to observational data on the size spread among young star-forming clusters in the galaxy SDSS J1226+2047 at redshift $z=0.0144$, we derive a constraint on $H_0$. When combined with a value of $H_0 = 69.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and corresponding cosmological parameters that generate a 5-year age disparity between young star clusters in our target galaxy, the analysis supports a $H_0$ variation consistent with a $\sim$3.5\% uncertainty under a linearized approximation. Consequently, by integrating our findings with prior research, we propose the feasibility of utilizing our methodology to probe $H_0$ and its spatial fluctuations on relatively large, Mpc-scale distances.
